title: Military & Defense
tagline: Enlisted and officer paths, technical training, and the transition to civilian careers.
summary: Military service is a structured career with paid training, clear ranks, and benefits that extend into civilian life — across dozens of occupational fields from aviation to medicine to logistics. This roadmap covers joining (ASVAB, MEPS, branches), serving (training, promotion, education), and transitioning out deliberately.

sources.label: O*NET — Military Officer Special and Tactical Operations Leaders (55-1011.00)

detail.description: The US military has six branches (Army, Navy, Air Force, Marines, Space Force, Coast Guard), each with enlisted, warrant officer, and commissioned officer tracks across hundreds of job fields.
detail.why: Service offers paid training, housing, healthcare, education benefits, and a promotion ladder — with a commitment of years and real obligations to weigh honestly.
learn: Compare the six branches' missions and cultures
Learn enlisted vs warrant vs officer tracks
Talk to veterans from two branches
List what you want the military to train you for

detail.description: Enlisted members perform and lead hands-on specialties; officers (requiring a bachelor's or academy path) lead and manage; warrant officers are technical experts between.
detail.why: The track choice shapes your entire service — education level, daily work, pay, and promotion speed all differ.
learn: Compare duties, pay, and requirements per track
Check degree requirements for officer paths
Note the warrant-officer technical-expert lane
Decide which track fits your education and goals

detail.description: The Armed Services Vocational Aptitude Battery tests math, verbal, and technical aptitude — your scores determine which military jobs you qualify for.
detail.why: ASVAB scores open or close job fields; preparing seriously expands your options before you ever sign.
learn: Take a full practice ASVAB for a baseline
Drill math and word knowledge daily for 4–8 weeks
Learn which line scores gate your target jobs
Retake to improve if needed (rules apply)

detail.description: Enlistment contracts run typically 4–6 years with obligations beyond; in exchange: salary, housing allowances, healthcare, the GI Bill, and pension systems for long service.
detail.why: Understanding the full contract — and the benefits earned — lets you use service as a deliberate life strategy.
learn: Read a sample enlistment contract with a recruiter
Learn the GI Bill's education benefits
Understand housing allowance basics (BAH)
Note pension vesting for career service

detail.description: Recruiters guide entry but represent their branch: talk to several branches, get job and bonus promises IN WRITING, and never sign for an unspecified 'open' contract without understanding it.
detail.why: Your first job field shapes your whole service — written guarantees are the only protection.
learn: Meet recruiters from 3 branches
Get your target job in your contract in writing
Ask veterans about their recruiter experience
Negotiate for training, not just bonuses

detail.description: The Military Entrance Processing Station: medical examination, ASVAB verification, and contract oath — where medical history disclosure matters enormously.
detail.why: Nondisclosure of medical history is fraud and can end service early; full disclosure protects you.
learn: Assemble complete medical records beforehand
Disclose everything — waivers exist for many conditions
Understand the oath and its legal weight
Prepare physically for the fitness baseline

detail.description: Military job fields mirror the civilian economy: aviation maintenance, medicine, logistics, IT, mechanical trades, intelligence, and combat arms — each with its own training pipeline.
detail.why: Choosing a field that teaches transferable civilian skills is the single best career decision in service.
learn: List job fields matching civilian careers you'd want
Compare training length and certification outcomes
Ask veterans which fields transition best
Pick based on skills-earned, not bonuses alone

detail.description: Basic training (7–13 weeks by branch) builds fitness, discipline, teamwork, and standards under stress — the shared foundation every member earns.
detail.why: Arriving physically prepared and mentally ready turns boot camp from a shock into a starting gun.
learn: Train to exceed your branch's fitness standards
Learn rank structure and customs beforehand
Practice the run times and push-up standards
Talk to recent graduates about the reality

detail.description: After basic, job schools teach your specialty — often with civilian-recognized certifications embedded (aviation maintenance, medical, IT credentials).
detail.why: Technical schools are where service starts paying career dividends: certifications and skills employers recognize.
learn: Identify civilian certifications in your field's school
Take the certification exams while training
Keep copies of every transcript
Network with instructors — they know the industry

detail.description: Service life: duty stations, deployments, exercises, and the rhythm of military schedules — excellence is reliability, fitness, and technical mastery over years.
detail.why: Promotion boards reward consistent performance records — every evaluation is permanent history.
learn: Build your service record deliberately (awards, quals, courses)
Maintain fitness standards without drama
Find mentors at the next rank
Volunteer for schools and deployments that teach

detail.description: Promotion is point-based: fitness scores, weapons quals, education, awards, and boards — officers advance through assignments and leadership evaluations.
detail.why: The system is transparent — studying it lets you control what's controllable instead of guessing.
learn: Learn your branch's promotion-point system
Maximize the controllable categories early
Study for promotion boards proactively
Track your own record file's accuracy

detail.description: Tuition Assistance funds degrees during service; CLEP/DSST exams grant credit free; and GI Bill benefits stack for after — education is a core military benefit.
detail.why: Members who graduate or certify while serving separate into far better civilian options.
learn: Use Tuition Assistance — it's separate from the GI Bill
Take CLEP exams for free college credit
Keep transcripts from every school and school-house
Plan degrees with an education counselor

detail.description: Military aviation spans pilots (officer-heavy, rigorous flight training), aircrew, and the maintenance fields that keep aircraft flying — among the most transferable technical pipelines.
detail.why: Military aviation experience converts directly to airline and maintenance careers — a famous and proven pipeline.
learn: Compare pilot vs aircrew vs maintenance paths
Note flight-school selection requirements
Log every flight hour and certification
Research civilian conversion for your aviation role

detail.description: Military medicine trains combat medics/corpsmen and technicians — experience that maps to EMT-paramedic, nursing, and clinical careers through documented equivalency paths.
detail.why: Medic experience is among the most respected medical training anywhere — with certification bridges to civilian licensure.
learn: Compare medic/corpsman training to civilian EMS levels
Research state equivalency for military medical training
Plan NREMT bridging if targeting EMS
Keep patient-care documentation for licensing boards

detail.description: Transition begins 12–24 months before separation: the mandatory transition program, resume translation, certification bridging, and job networking — planned transitions land far better jobs.
detail.why: The military-to-civilian jump is the field's defining challenge — those who start early, land well.
learn: Attend the transition program early, not at the deadline
Translate your MOS into civilian job language
Get certifications before separation
Network with veterans in your target industry

detail.description: The Post-9/11 GI Bill pays tuition, housing, and books for degrees — and transfers to dependents in some cases — one of the most valuable benefits earned in service.
detail.why: Using the GI Bill deliberately (right degree, right school, housing strategy) can set up an entire second career.
learn: Check your GI Bill eligibility and remaining months
Choose schools by outcome and Yellow Ribbon participation
Understand the housing stipend mechanics
Consider transfer-to-dependents rules if applicable

detail.description: Federal hiring gives eligible veterans preference points and special hiring authorities — plus the whole federal system values service-derived skills and clearance eligibility.
detail.why: Government careers are the natural first civilian landing — preference makes qualified veterans genuinely competitive.
learn: Learn veterans' preference rules on USAJOBS
Translate your record into federal resume format
Note clearance eligibility as an asset
Explore the big federal employers for your field

detail.description: An active or recently-held security clearance is a scarce, valuable credential — defense contractors and agencies pay premiums for cleared professionals.
detail.why: Clearances take time and money employers otherwise must sponsor — a serving member's clearance is real market value.
learn: Keep your record clean — clearances check everything
Know your clearance level and expiry window
Target cleared-employer job boards during transition
Maintain reporting obligations even after service

detail.description: Service ladder: recruit → specialist → NCO/officer → senior leadership; civilian continuation: federal service, defense contracting, skilled trades, aviation, medicine, or entrepreneurship.
detail.why: The military career is a first career that funds and trains the second — planning both together is the professional move.
learn: Sketch your 20-year plan including service years
Decide career-service vs one-enlistment strategy honestly
Build civilian skills during every assignment
Revisit the plan at each reenlistment point

detail.description: Service demands include deployments, family separation, and exposures that affect some members deeply — support systems exist and using them is strength, not weakness.
detail.why: The healthiest careers belong to members who use their support systems early — for themselves and their families.
learn: Learn your branch's mental-health resources
Build family support plans before deployments
Normalize counseling — it's routine in modern service
Keep connections outside the military alive

detail.description: Officer entry routes: service academies (highly competitive, free, service commitment), ROTC (degree + program), OCS (degree holders), and direct-commission for professionals (doctors, lawyers, chaplains).
detail.why: The officer path doubles leadership scope and pay — with four distinct doors depending on your stage of life.
learn: Compare academy, ROTC, and OCS timelines
Note degree and age requirements per route
Meet an officer recruiter for route planning
Weigh leadership training vs technical depth
